Introduction/Product implementation

Product implementation

Product implementation turns agreed product intent into software that can be tested, released and operated. Start with the product requirements document (PRD), relevant user interface (UI) artefacts and known constraints. Build a small change, verify it against the acceptance criteria, observe its behaviour and use the evidence to choose the next change.

It is written for product owners, architects, engineers and reviewers working in the same squad. The stages, gates and practices below are a working model for this guide, and the examples are fictional. Confirm stage names and decision authority against the agreed lifecycle before relying on them.

Where implementation starts

Product implementation is the second of two separate loops. Product ideation tests whether the proposed product addresses a worthwhile problem. Product implementation checks whether the software behaves as intended in the conditions it will encounter. Neither loop removes all uncertainty.

Read the diagram from left to right. Ideation ends with a commitment decision and hands off a PRD and UI artefacts. The implementation loop, highlighted in blue, builds from that handoff, releases the product and keeps refining it. Learning from use returns to ideation when it changes the product intent rather than only its delivery.

Enter implementation when the next change has agreed behaviour and testable acceptance criteria. For a bounded defect or maintenance change, a reviewed issue may be enough. Return to ideation and its handoff checks when delivery evidence challenges user value or intended behaviour; resolve technical unknowns through focused investigation.

How the implementation loop works

Implementation is not a one-way handoff from requirements to code. It is a governed loop: it converts intent into production behaviour, observes what happens, and uses that evidence to choose the next change. Each increment is both a product change and a test of how the team delivers.

Read the top row from left to right and the bottom row from right to left. The readiness package feeds Plan, which produces the technical requirements document (TRD). Slice breaks the TRD into small tasks, and Implement produces each change with its evidence. Verify, highlighted in blue, is done by someone or something other than the implementer; findings send the change back for rework. Release and observe moves it into real conditions, and Learn chooses the next refinement. Evidence can return work to any earlier stage, not only the one before.

Improve two things at once

The loop improves two systems:

  • The product: its usefulness, usability, reliability, safety, performance, cost and fit with users’ work.
  • The software factory: the context, task breakdown, agent instructions, tools, tests, reviews, release controls, monitoring and recovery that produce the product.

The same failure often needs both responses. A local fix restores the current increment; a change to the delivery process aims to prevent recurrence and is checked on later increments. Read about software factories.

Record the evidence and next decision

  • Defined inputs and outputs make each transition inspectable and reusable.
  • Evidence requirements separate demonstrated behaviour from assertion.
  • Exit decisions state who or what can authorise progress.
  • Traceability links product intent to decisions, tasks, tests, releases and outcomes.
  • Feedback paths let evidence revise the PRD, TRD, context, tasks, tests, tools or policies.

Start from the PRD and UI artefacts

Implementation begins with a minimum package that lets people and agents work from the same intent and constraints. The PRD and UI artefacts come from ideation. Organisational context comes from the architecture, policy and domain owners who constrain what a valid implementation is.

Minimum implementation-readiness package
InputMinimum contentEvidence it is ready
PRDProblem, target users, scope, user stories, acceptance criteria, non-functional requirements, dependencies and exclusionsAn accountable owner is named, assumptions are visible and acceptance criteria are testable
UI artefactsRepresentative HTML screens and a design.md file covering interaction rules, states, responsive behaviour, accessibility and intentional deviationsCritical journeys can be walked end to end, including loading, empty, error, permission and responsive states
Organisational contextArchitecture, business, domain, policy, security, data, operational and technical constraintsContext is current, authoritative, scoped, attributable and available to each agent that needs it

For services without a user interface, use API or event contracts and representative interactions instead of screens. Apply the package to the scope being changed; it does not require every product decision to be settled before implementation starts.

Let the PRD define intent, not design

The PRD sets the problem boundary, desired outcomes, observable behaviour and constraints, and leaves legitimate implementation choices to the TRD. A PRD that dictates internal design suppresses engineering judgement. A PRD without acceptance criteria forces implementers to invent product policy. Both create hidden risk.

Note

If the product itself contains an AI capability, the PRD also needs its probabilistic behaviour, failure modes, human fallback, prohibited outcomes, data use, evaluation populations and quality thresholds. Deterministic rules need hard passes; probabilistic behaviour needs agreed evaluation sets and thresholds.

Use UI artefacts to make behaviour concrete

HTML screens show layout, navigation, content density and important states. The design.md file records what pixels alone cannot keep: interaction rules, responsive breakpoints, accessibility semantics, design tokens and design decisions. When the experience changes, update the artefacts, acceptance criteria and related tests together.

Treat organisational context as part of the specification

Architecture standards, domain rules, policies, security controls, operating constraints and business priorities define what a valid implementation is. Without them, an agent can produce work that is correct locally but incompatible with the wider system.

Before planning, an accountable owner should confirm that the package is coherent enough to plan from. Material unknowns should be either resolved or carried as bounded assumptions, each with an owner and a review date.

Next step: walk one critical journey through your UI artefacts, including its error and permission states. Check that each state has a matching acceptance criterion in the PRD.

Translate intent into executable work

Specification-driven development makes expected behaviour and design decisions explicit before implementation. GitHub Spec Kit describes a specification, planning and task workflow; this guide uses PRD and TRD as its local document names. The PRD defines required outcomes, the TRD records how the system will deliver them, and tasks turn those commitments into small units that can be verified. Read about spec-driven development.

From product intent to executable work
LayerQuestion it answersMain contentsQuality test
PRDWhat outcome and behaviour are required?Problem, users, scope, stories, acceptance criteria, non-functional requirements, dependencies, exclusionsDoes the team agree what success means?
TRDHow will the system deliver that behaviour?Architecture, interfaces, data, identity, security, operations, rollout, monitoring, trade-offsAre key decisions explicit, feasible and reviewable?
TasksWhich small changes will create and verify it?Vertical slices, dependencies, tests, evidence, review routes, completion criteriaCan each task be completed and verified without reinventing intent?

Use the TRD as a decision record

A strong TRD explains the affected components, integration boundaries, data flows, API or event contracts, storage, identity and authorisation, failure handling, monitoring, performance, migration, rollout, rollback and unresolved risks. Each major decision traces to the PRD requirement it serves. Recording non-goals, alternatives considered and rejected trade-offs stops later tasks from silently redesigning the system.

Write tasks as units of verification

A task is ready when it describes a bounded change in behaviour and makes completion independently decidable. Each task should carry:

  • links to the PRD acceptance criteria and TRD decisions it implements;
  • a precise change boundary, such as the affected component, interface or user journey;
  • dependencies, sequencing constraints and the approved execution environment;
  • the unit, integration, end-to-end and non-functional checks its risk requires;
  • the expected evidence, such as test results, screenshots, evaluations or performance measurements; and
  • its independent review route and the person who accepts it.

Give each agent enough context, and no more

Relevant context helps an agent work within the intended scope, but does not guarantee correct output. Manage context like a product: versioned, attributable, scoped to a domain or repository, discoverable and checked for freshness. Give an agent enough to make the current decision, then disclose deeper guidance only when the task, risk or uncertainty justifies it. Log what context and tools were used, so reviewers can reconstruct what informed an outcome. Read about context engineering.

Next step: pick one task in your backlog. Check that it links to an acceptance criterion and a TRD decision, and that someone other than its implementer could decide whether it is done.

Run the six stages

The six stages are this guide’s working model, not a prescribed organisational lifecycle. Each has a purpose, expected evidence and an exit decision. Scale the documentation and reviews to the change’s risk.

The six stages of the implementation loop
StagePurposeEvidence producedExit decision
1. PlanDecide how the intent will be delivered within organisational constraints, and challenge contradictionsReviewed TRD, decision records, risk register, requirement traceabilityThe required owners agree the approach is feasible and material risks have an accepted treatment
2. SliceBreak the TRD into small vertical tasks that can be built, tested and reviewed on their ownTask graph, verification contracts, environment needs, review plan, release sequenceEvery task is implementable, traceable and small enough to keep change and evidence together
3. ImplementProduce the smallest coherent increment, test-first and with narrow changesChange set, tests, integration proof, UI evidence, evaluations, scanner results, updated documentationThe implementer has resolved or explained findings and assembled evidence for review; this is not final validation
4. VerifyTest and review the increment independently of the person or agent that made itAttributable review results, full test report, mutation result where used, exceptions, consolidated quality reportIndependent reviewers pass the change and an accountable person accepts the quality report and remaining risk
5. Release and observeMove the increment into real conditions while limiting the blast radiusDeployment record, telemetry, incidents, support signals, experiment results, adoption, recovery evidenceThe increment is stable within thresholds, or has been contained or rolled back
6. LearnTurn outcomes into controlled changes to the product and the factoryDecision log, revised PRD or TRD, new tasks, updated context and skills, preventive controlsAn accountable owner chooses the next refinement and provides an updated definition

In Learn, compare what happened with the PRD’s outcomes and the TRD’s assumptions, and separate product causes from factory causes. If the evidence shows the product intent was wrong, not just its delivery, return it to the ideation loop.

Next step: for the change your team is working on now, name its current stage and write down the exit decision it needs next, including who makes it.

Govern progress with gates and independent checks

An exit gate is not a meeting or a status label. It evaluates named evidence against named criteria and records who made the decision. Automated gates suit deterministic rules, such as tests passing, schema compatibility, dependency policy and vulnerability severity. People are needed for judgement, trade-offs, risk acceptance and product interpretation.

A strong gate records the evidence it evaluated, the policy version, blocking and advisory findings, exceptions, the approver, the time and the next permitted action. That record lets the team give agents more autonomy without losing the ability to audit what happened.

Separate correction from assurance

Use two complementary checks. In the inner loop, sensors and scanners give the implementer fast feedback on their own work. In the outer loop, independent reviewers decide whether the work is acceptable. Self-review provides useful feedback, but does not replace the agreed acceptance decision.

On the left, the implementer runs sensors and scanners and fixes what they find. Sensors include compilers, type checks, linters, static analysis, secret detection, dependency scanning, policy checks, contract tests, accessibility checks, model evaluations and performance smoke tests. The implementer then passes its evidence to specialist reviewers, chosen by the change’s risk, such as security, privacy, performance, architecture, UI fidelity, accessibility and test quality. A review orchestrator consolidates their findings and sends blocking ones back for rework. The accountable person, highlighted in blue, accepts the quality report and authorises the release scope.

Separation of duties; confirm roles and authority locally
RoleCanShould not do alone
Implementation agentCreate changes, run tests and scanners, fix findings and assemble evidenceAccept its own work or suppress independent blocking findings
Specialist review agentReview within a defined remit, reproduce evidence, raise findings and confirm fixesApprove outside its remit or accept business risk
Review orchestratorRoute reviews, merge duplicate findings, track closure and compile the quality reportTurn unresolved disagreement into a silent pass
Accountable personWeigh trade-offs, accept the quality report and approve exceptions and remaining riskDelegate accountability without a policy and an audit trail

Make verification independent in practice

A second agent can repeat the first agent’s assumptions. Have a reviewer check acceptance criteria against the original user need, reproduce results, and inspect changes to tests as well as code. Keep release permissions outside the implementer’s control. Independence depends on evidence and permissions, not the number of agents.

Build testing into implementation

Unit tests give fast feedback on local behaviour, integration tests check contracts with dependencies, and end-to-end tests protect critical user journeys. Choose the mix by the change’s risk and architecture; no single layer is enough.

  • Use test-driven development to define the expected behaviour before implementing it.
  • Use characterisation tests to capture existing behaviour in legacy or high-risk areas before changing it.
  • Use mutation testing, where it is worthwhile, to check whether the tests would catch meaningful faults. Line coverage alone is weak assurance.
  • Treat failing tests as diagnostic evidence, and flaky tests as defects with an owner and a plan to remove them.
  • Make test data, dependencies, models, prompts and environment settings reproducible enough for an independent reviewer.

Evaluate AI behaviour across repeated trials

This applies when evaluating a development agent or a product that contains AI. Anthropic’s agent evaluation guidance distinguishes a task, repeated trials, grading and the actual outcome. It recommends combining executable checks, model-based assessment and human judgement where each fits.

Record the dataset, model, instructions, tools and environment used. Repeat representative tasks because outputs can vary. Check final state and side effects, not only the agent’s response. Calibrate model-based graders against human judgements, and keep regression cases for failures already fixed.

For the service desk assistant, include unsupported questions, restricted information and escalation cases. Report failures by case type, alongside completion, latency and cost; an overall pass rate can hide a serious failure. Agree the acceptance rule before running the evaluation.

A minimum quality report brings together the linked PRD acceptance criteria, test and evaluation results, scanner and policy findings, open exceptions or remaining risk, and the accountable person’s decision for the defined release scope.

Next step: look at the last change your team merged. Identify who, other than its author, decided it was acceptable, and where that decision is recorded.

Provide tools, context and execution controls

The platform should make safe execution the easiest path. It gives people and agents consistent access to authorised context, reusable procedures, tools, realistic dependencies and standard commands, and keeps the evidence needed to reconstruct each action.

Minimum platform capabilities for the implementation loop
CapabilityWhat it provides and controls
Context platformCurrent organisational, architecture, domain, policy, security and technical context, with source, version, owner, freshness and access control
Skills registryTested, reusable procedures, each with a version, an owner, dependencies, evaluations and a retirement status
Tool gatewayGoverned access to tools, data and services through Model Context Protocol (MCP) or similar, with identity, allow-lists, rate limits, audit trails and data boundaries
Test containersReproducible dependencies such as databases, queues, browsers, services and models, with pinned versions and isolated data
Standard command-line and CI toolingThe same build, test, review, packaging, release and recovery commands locally and in continuous integration (CI), with structured output and meaningful exit codes
AI gatewayGoverned model access, with allow-lists, routing, authentication, model-version records, safety controls, data-residency enforcement and cost records

Design the platform around these principles:

  • Least privilege: grant access scoped to the task, and raise it only through policy-controlled routes.
  • Predictable interfaces: prefer structured inputs, machine-readable outputs, meaningful exit codes and operations that are safe to repeat.
  • Provenance throughout: keep the specifications, context versions, tools, models, prompts, code, tests, reviewers and approvals behind each outcome.
  • Safe isolation: run untrusted changes in disposable environments with synthetic or approved data.
  • Readable evidence: produce quality reports that accountable people can understand and challenge.
  • Replaceable parts: put context, skills, models, scanners and tool providers behind stable contracts.

Increase autonomy only with evidence

A mature factory is not one without people. It is one whose chosen way of working produces acceptable outcomes with the right control, evidence and recovery. Different products, and different kinds of change, can work at different levels in the same organisation.

Three ways to run the factory; each is a risk choice
ModeRole of peopleControls neededGood fit
AI as co-pilotPeople drive the work; agents suggest, generate, explain and checkNormal engineering controls, review of agent output, clear data and tool boundariesNew work, uncertain requirements, sensitive design, decisions needing high judgement
Light factoryAgents run substantial workflows; people handle exceptions and accept quality reportsStrong specifications, automated tests, specialist review, monitoring, rollback, traceabilityRepeatable delivery where risk is bounded and evidence is mature
Dark factoryPeople set goals, policy and escalation limits; routine work proceeds without themProven autonomy, formal risk classification, independent automated assurance, strict tool control, containment, auditabilityHighly standardised, unambiguous work with stable architecture, strong tests, small blast radius and proven recovery

Choose autonomy that serves the task and fits the available evidence and controls. More autonomy is not itself an improvement. Weigh safety and regulatory impact, data sensitivity, reversibility, blast radius, product ambiguity, architecture stability, test strength, monitoring, recovery time, model reliability and risk tolerance.

Grant autonomy per kind of action. For example, an agent might update a dependency within a tested range, while a schema migration or a policy change still needs explicit approval. Raise autonomy only after sustained evidence, and reduce it automatically when control health, quality or recovery gets worse.

Note

Running without people is not the same as maturity. A dark factory without independent assurance, containment, monitoring and proven recovery is an unattended risk. Read about light and dark software factories.

Measure whether the whole loop works

No single measure shows whether delivery is improving. Speed can improve while escaped defects, policy exceptions or harm to users increase. Balance measures across flow, quality, recovery, product outcomes, system health and governance.

Suggested measures; set local measures and thresholds before relying on them
FamilyExample signalsQuestion it answers
FlowLead time, cycle time, work in progress, gate wait time, review latency, deployment frequencyDoes valuable work move predictably, and where does evidence wait?
QualityFirst-pass review rate, escaped defects, mutation score, change failure rate, evaluation pass rateDoes the loop prevent and detect important failures?
RecoveryTime to detect, contain, restore and prevent recurrence; rollback success; repeat defectsCan the team limit harm and learn quickly when something fails?
ProductAdoption, task success, retention, time saved, satisfaction, error rate, harm and fairness indicatorsIs the product solving the intended user problem?
System healthAvailability, latency, cost per outcome, data quality, flaky tests, context freshness, tool failuresCan the product and factory sustain the required service?
GovernanceTraceability, policy coverage, gate bypasses, exception age, approval latency, unauthorised tool attemptsIs autonomy operating within its declared authority and risk tolerance?

Lines of code, prompts issued and tasks attempted are weak measures of productivity. Measure the flow of accepted product behaviour instead: how quickly well-defined intent becomes a safe increment, how often it is rejected or fails, whether users benefit and whether the factory improves after learning. Split measures by risk, product area, type of change and factory mode.

Use consistent delivery measures

DORA’s current delivery guidance uses five measures: change lead time, deployment frequency, failed deployment recovery time, change fail rate and deployment rework rate. Lead time runs from commit to production; recovery time concerns a failed deployment requiring intervention. Rework rate tracks unplanned deployments caused by production incidents.

Follow one application or service over time using consistent definitions. Pair delivery measures with user outcomes and operating cost. Do not rank individuals by these measures or attribute a change to AI without checking other changes in scope, staffing and process.

Agree the response before the signal arrives

The following are suggested responses to investigate and adapt locally:

  • Review latency above its target leads to more review capacity, smaller tasks or a simpler review policy.
  • Recurring defects lead to factory fixes, such as new scanner rules, better tests, updated skills or corrected context.
  • A falling mutation score prompts a review of changed tests and code before increasing autonomy, even when line coverage stays high.
  • Repeated gate bypasses lead to a governance review and can reduce autonomy automatically.
  • Worsening product outcomes with stable system health lead to refining the PRD or experience, not infrastructure work.
  • Recovery outside tolerance leads to stronger containment before deployment frequency increases.

Put the loop into practice

The loop becomes real when its controls are part of daily work. The sequence below is a suggested starting point; automate it step by step while keeping decision authority visible.

  1. Classify the change. Record its product area, risk, factory mode, required evidence, reviewers and decision authority.
  2. Confirm readiness. Check the PRD, UI artefacts and organisational context, and record bounded assumptions with owners.
  3. Approve the TRD. Trace decisions to requirements and complete the architecture, security, policy, data and operations reviews that apply.
  4. Slice the work vertically. Create small tasks with test obligations, expected evidence, dependencies and independent review routes.
  5. Implement test-first. Run sensors and scanners continuously, keep provenance, and keep the specification in step with the change.
  6. Run independent assurance. Carry out specialist reviews and the full test strategy; do not let the creator validate its own work.
  7. Accept the quality report. An accountable person accepts the remaining risk and authorises the release scope.
  8. Release progressively. Limit the blast radius, check health, keep a way to contain or roll back, and collect evidence.
  9. Close the learning loop. Update the product intent and factory controls, then check whether the change improved outcomes or prevented recurrence.

Define rollout and recovery before release

A canary release exposes a change to a limited portion of traffic before wider deployment. Google’s SRE Workbook explains how comparing a canary with the existing version can reveal failures that pre-release tests miss. It limits exposure; it does not guarantee a safe release.

Record the initial audience, observation period, health and user-outcome measures, stop thresholds, and the person or automation that can halt rollout. Rehearse recovery before expanding exposure. Where traffic is too low for a useful comparison, use a bounded pilot and direct observation.

Check whether recovery also needs to restore data or reverse external actions. Rolling back application code may not undo a migration, a sent message or an automated decision. For an AI capability, record the model, prompt and retrieval configuration with the release so the team can restore the intended combination.

Check pilot readiness

A team is ready to pilot the loop when:

  • the PRD contains testable user stories, acceptance criteria, non-functional requirements and exclusions;
  • the design.md file and HTML screens cover core journeys and their loading, empty, error, permission, accessibility and responsive states;
  • architecture, business, domain, policy, security and technical context is versioned, owned, accessible and current;
  • work can be sliced into small tasks with dependencies, risk, verification commands, completion evidence and traceability;
  • build agents run in constrained environments and cannot silently bypass repository, review or pipeline protections; and
  • end-to-end tests are derived from user stories and keep reproducible evidence for critical journeys.

Next step: go through the pilot readiness list with your squad and note each item you cannot yet confirm. Read how the EDS workflow runs the loop.

Run the loop with the EDS workflow

The EDS AI Development Workflow: Simplified Operating Handbook describes how EDS turns a validated PRD into released software: a governed workflow in which each stage produces a recorded artefact, and people approve the decisions that carry risk. This section summarises that handbook for developers and reviewers.

In this page’s terms, the handbook’s planning sequence covers Plan and Slice, its convergence loop covers Implement, and its independent verification and closeout cover Verify. Its release-readiness checks prepare the release decision. This mapping is an editorial reading, not the handbook’s own structure.

The skills, gates and default thresholds below are as stated in the handbook. Some skills are marked there as planned rather than available. Check the current handbook version and your team’s configuration before relying on a specific gate or command.

Seven operating principles

The handbook summarises the workflow in seven principles:

  1. Provide context before important decisions. Make business goals, architecture, policy and coding constraints available early.
  2. Load only what is relevant. Reveal standards progressively instead of placing the whole knowledge base in every prompt.
  3. Use AI as the first reviewer. Challenge generated plans, specifications and tickets before accepting them.
  4. Secure the design before coding. Treat architecture and compliance as early checks, not late clean-up.
  5. Slice work vertically. Each task delivers a demonstrable outcome across the layers it needs, rather than a separate batch of schema, API or interface work.
  6. Build self-correction into implementation. Implement, review, validate and correct repeatedly until the work converges.
  7. Keep people accountable for intent and risk. Automation can do the work; people approve compliance, execution readiness and release.

Follow the workflow from PRD to release

The workflow moves from business intent to a compliance-approved technical contract, then to execution-ready slices of work, implementation, independent verification and a human release decision.

Read the top row from left to right and the bottom row from right to left. The product owner (PO) or business analyst (BA) hands over the PRD. The architect or Tech Lead turns it into a technical requirements document (TRD) and has it challenged. Human-in-the-loop gate 1 (HITL 1) approves its compliance; unresolved findings send the TRD back for revision. The work is then sliced into vertical issues, and HITL 2 approves them as ready to build or returns them for rework. A developer or agent builds one slice at a time in the convergence loop. Independent verification either passes the slice or returns it for correction, and the Tech Lead decides whether to release.

Note

The handbook treats HITL 1 and HITL 2 as decisions that cannot be delegated to an agent. HITL 1 approves compliance before the TRD is broken into issues. HITL 2 approves issue quality and execution readiness before implementation begins.

The handbook labels each step and skill with a status:

Status labels used in the EDS handbook and in the tables below
LabelMeaning
CoreExpected in the normal sequence.
RecommendedOptional, but skipping it reduces confidence or quality.
OptionalCan be skipped when the cost and risk are understood.
PlannedDescribed but not yet implemented. Do not use it as a live gate until it has been verified.
HITLA person approves before the workflow advances.

Know who owns each contract

The PRD and the TRD are different agreements with different owners. The PRD states what the product needs to do and why. The TRD adds how it fits the architecture, the codebase and the applicable policies. The handbook treats the visual reference as optional, whereas this guide’s handoff includes UI artefacts; confirm locally which applies.

PRD and TRD compared, as described in the EDS handbook
ArtefactAccountable roleContainsComplete when
PRDPO / BABusiness intent, user stories, acceptance criteria, scope and an optional visual referenceCommitted and handed to the development team
TRDArchitect / Tech LeadTechnical constraints, architecture decision records (ADRs), codebase context, domain-model alignment and implementation implicationsCompliance-approved and ready to break into issues
Role boundaries and handoffs in the EDS handbook
RoleStarts withOwnsHands off
PO / BAA business problem or opportunityDiscovery, requirements, acceptance criteria and visual referencePRD and specification files, with an optional prototype
Architect / Tech LeadThe PO / BA handoffDependencies, TRD, ADRs, policies, architecture tests and vertical decompositionApproved, execution-ready issues
DeveloperThe highest-priority ready issueThe implementation loop, tests, review evidence and closeoutA merge-ready merge request (MR) with acceptance evidence
Tech Lead / reviewersThe MR and release candidateSpecification and standards review, risk acceptance and production sign-offAn approved merge or release decision

Architects and Tech Leads hand over an approved queue, not only a decomposed backlog. Each issue has been challenged, checked against policy, sliced vertically and labelled ready for execution.

Plan and break down the work

Planning turns the PRD into a challenged, compliance-checked design and then into small issues. The handbook calls each issue a tracer bullet: a thin vertical slice that reaches an observable outcome through every technical layer it needs.

Planning and detailing sequence in the EDS handbook
StepSkill or actionWhat it produces
Optional/backwards-mappingA map from value to entry points, boundaries and vertical slices; use it when uncertainty is high.
1/setup-matt-pocock-skillsTracker, triage labels and domain layout, configured once per repository.
2/dependency-orchestratorA story dependency graph, delivery schedule, PM Report and Dev Delivery Plan.
3 · PlannedContext7 MCPCurrent, version-specific library documentation when a specific API claim arises.
4/arch-tests-plan, then /arch-tests-genArchitecture rules turned into executable boundary tests.
5/wayfinder with the relevant standardsResolved domain, codebase, dependency and design constraints.
6/to-spec, then /grill-meA published TRD whose assumptions and gaps have been challenged.
7/spec-complianceEvidence of the TRD’s compliance with IM8, ARC and other registered policies.
HITL 1Human compliance sign-offFindings resolved and the TRD approved; required before ticket decomposition.
8/to-tickets, then /grill-meDependency-ordered tracer-bullet issues.
9/issue-verification and /fry-meIssues checked for verticality, demonstrability, size and specification quality.
HITL 2Human execution-readiness sign-offQuestions resolved and issues marked ready; the queue can enter implementation.

In the handbook’s glossary, IM8 refers to application technical security controls and ARC to agentic AI governance controls, both from the supplied policy set. Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a way of connecting an agent to external tools and knowledge.

An issue is execution-ready when:

  • it delivers an observable increment of user or system value;
  • it covers the technical layers it needs, instead of splitting schema, API or interface work into unrelated batches;
  • its dependencies and blocking relationships are explicit;
  • its acceptance criteria are specific enough for automated or browser verification;
  • it is small enough for a manageable implementation loop, without hidden follow-up work; and
  • the applicable standards and policy implications are linked to it.

Two practices support this planning. Standards are stored as small, indexed concept files, so each story loads only the few standards it needs. Architecture rules become build-time tests, such as ArchUnit or dependency-cruiser rules, so generated code that breaks a layer or dependency rule fails the build instead of drifting silently.

Run the convergence loop

A developer, or an agent working for one, builds each ready issue with the /do-work skill. The handbook describes three ways to run it:

Execution modes in the EDS handbook
ModeWho operates itHow it worksBest fit
1. Local interactiveDeveloperThe developer pair-programs with /do-work and owns branches and decisions.Complex or ambiguous work that needs frequent judgement
2. Local autonomousLocal agentAn isolated sandbox checks out, implements and commits locally.Well-specified slices with controlled local autonomy
3. Cloud or CI autonomousManaged runnerA pipeline picks a ready issue, runs /do-work, pushes code, opens an MR and triggers review.Repeatable, unattended execution at scale

Before the first code change, /do-work agrees a sprint contract for the session. The contract records the feature and its intended behaviour; the files or modules in scope and those out of scope; dependencies and governing standards; validation commands and the runtime evidence required; and time or token limits, escalation triggers and stop criteria.

The sprint contract feeds the loop. Implement the smallest end-to-end slice using test-driven development (TDD) and the applicable standards. Review with /code-reviewer and, where configured, mutation testing: deliberately introduce faults to check whether the tests detect them.

Run the configured gates. If a gate fails or a blocking finding remains, diagnose the cause and correct the change. A passing exit condition completes the loop. Reaching the session’s time or token limit, encountering a blocker, or needing additional authority instead stops work for escalation; none of these means the slice has passed.

Gates inside the loop, with the handbook’s default thresholds; teams can set their own
GateChecksDefault rule
Build and testFormatting, type checking or compilation, unit and integration tests, production build, coverageTests and build pass; coverage at least 80% unless team policy differs
Quality and complianceSemgrep, IM8, maintainability, framework and standards checks as applicableCritical or High findings block the commit; must-fix findings reach zero
MutationMutation testing on changed filesKill rate at least 70%, tuned to the team’s risk
ArchitectureProject and feature boundary testsNo prohibited dependency or layer violations

Verify functional behaviour first, then resilience and performance, and only then style or refactoring. Do not widen the scope of the change while its core behaviour is still failing.

Prove completion independently

An agent that reports “done” has not shown that the work is done. The handbook requires a deterministic command, an independent reviewer or a separate evaluator to decide whether the stop condition is met; the developer agent is never the only judge.

The three layers answer different questions. Syntax and structure uses build, static analysis and boundary-test output. Behaviour uses unit, integration and feature verification tests, including negative and boundary cases. System uses browser or API end-to-end (E2E) tests, health checks, logs, traces and screenshots. The independent judge, highlighted in blue, decides: the slice either moves to closeout or returns to the loop.

Closeout sequence in the EDS handbook
ActionStatusPurpose
/improve-codebase-architectureRecommendedFind shallow modules and deepen them where worthwhile.
/arch-tests-gen-featureCoreCreate boundary tests for the slice’s real packages or folders.
Push, open MR, /code-reviewCoreReview the change against both standards and the specification.
/diagnosing-bugsRecommendedDiagnose failures or regressions from evidence.
/browser-testRecommendedRun live acceptance scenarios and keep screenshot evidence.
/flaky-test-detectorPlannedRepeat E2E scenarios three to five times and block inconsistent results.
/git-commit-skillRecommendedGroup remaining changes into logical Conventional Commits.
/gen-uat-scriptsPlannedGenerate user acceptance testing (UAT) scripts from PRD acceptance criteria.
Human lead reviewHITLApprove and merge to the release branch.

Under the handbook’s closeout criteria, the slice satisfies its approved issue without unrelated changes. Applicable gates pass, blocking findings are resolved, and standards are followed or exceptions recorded. The merge request links acceptance evidence and boundary tests, explains remaining risks, and records the next action. For interface work, also check visual fidelity, end-to-end interaction, loading, empty and error states, accessibility, and behaviour across supported viewports and zoom levels.

Load the right context at each stage

AI output depends on the context it receives. The handbook asks for context that is explicit, versioned, selective and traceable to the decision it influenced, and loads different sources at different stages.

Context loaded at each stage, as described in the EDS handbook
StageContext loadedLoaded byWhy
Architecture and designShared standards, recipes, ADR templates, legacy constraints/dependency-orchestrator, /wayfinderStops a flawed design from spreading into tickets
Compliance and governanceRegulatory, security and AI governance policies/spec-complianceMakes controls explicit before coding
ImplementationFramework guides, API documentation, coding practices/do-work through /query-kbImproves syntax, patterns, buildability and tests
Merge reviewRepository style, naming, architecture and lint expectations/code-review with CODING_STANDARDS.mdKeeps changes consistent with the codebase

Search in order of precision: repository and text search for exact names, a code graph for call paths and dependencies, a knowledge base for meaning across standards and past decisions, and live documentation through MCP when a version-specific claim arises. Record decisions and progress in the repository before a long session is compacted; a larger context window does not replace durable state.

Note

Use the repository and executable checks to establish current behaviour. They do not override an applicable policy or approved requirement. When sources conflict, record the conflict and ask the responsible owner to resolve it before proceeding with the affected work.

Diagnose the harness when work fails

The harness is everything around the model: instructions, tools, environment, state and feedback. A capable model can still fail because one of these is weak. The handbook advises strengthening the weak layer rather than assuming the model is the only problem.

Start from the symptom and ask which of the five layers let it through. In the figure, verification feedback is the weak layer, so the team improves its checks rather than retrying the same prompt. Recording the failure helps the next session avoid it. The table pairs each layer with its typical symptom.

Harness layers, typical symptoms and responses, from the EDS handbook
LayerTypical symptomResponse
Task specificationPlausible implementation, wrong behaviourTighten the PRD or TRD, acceptance criteria, exclusions and slice scope.
Context provisionBreaks a domain, security, architecture or interface rule the agent could not seePut the rule in the repository and route it through the right context source.
Execution environmentTime lost on dependencies, connectivity or setupStandardise initialisation and keep a reproducible sandbox.
Verification feedbackThe agent reports “done”, but the behaviour is still brokenUse executable stop conditions, full-pipeline checks and actionable failure messages.
State managementA new session repeats work or reverses an earlier decisionRecord feature state, decisions, evidence, blockers and the next action.

Check release readiness

In the handbook, the Tech Lead reviews consolidated evidence and records the release decision before production. Confirm the applicable authority locally. The handbook describes a single /pre-prod-check orchestrator as planned; until it exists, run the component checks separately after confirming each one is installed. Its production sign-off checklist asks for:

  1. generated, reviewable API documentation;
  2. a reviewed authorisation matrix, with any unprotected endpoints intentional and approved;
  3. no unmitigated Critical or High vulnerabilities (CVEs) in dependencies;
  4. threat-model findings triaged and signed off;
  5. a current technical architecture document and dependency inventory;
  6. a passing full-codebase IM8 and ARC assessment, or documented risk acceptance;
  7. confirmed observability, secrets and configuration readiness; and
  8. the Tech Lead’s review of the evidence and recorded release decision.

To see whether the workflow itself is healthy, the handbook suggests watching measures such as:

  • Verified completion rate: how many started slices reach a passing state with independent evidence.
  • Verification gap: how often an agent’s claim of completion fails independent validation.
  • Rebuild cost: the time or tokens a fresh session needs to regain a working, informed state.
  • Tokens per verified slice: the cost of each independently passing feature, split by planning, implementation, verification and recovery.
  • Harness debt: stale, duplicated, contradictory or unenforced instructions and controls.

Example · fictional workflow run

The service desk squad’s access-request PRD reaches the Tech Lead, who drafts the TRD. /spec-compliance finds that the design logs full request text, so the TRD is revised to log request identifiers before HITL 1. The first tracer-bullet issue covers one journey: a staff member submits an access request and receives a drafted response. In the convergence loop, the mutation gate shows that no test checks the unauthorised-request case; the developer adds one. A browser test then provides the evidence the reviewer needs to approve the MR.

Next step: before your team uses the workflow on a live feature, confirm the one-time setup in the handbook: the tracker and its ready states are configured, the shared standards are available locally, CODING_STANDARDS.md reflects current conventions, and the generated architecture tests pass on the baseline branch.
